Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 3–4:

﴿Fussilat﴾ means "were made clear" (bayyanat). It was also said: "were divided" (qutti'at) into surahs and verses. ﴿A Qur'an in Arabic﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb in the sense of specification (al-takhsis), or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), or it is a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿For a people who know﴾ means: who know things and who understand the proofs when they reflect upon them, and that is the knowledge which makes the obligation (taklif) binding. It was also said: the meaning is "who know the truth and faith." The first is general and this is specific, and the first is preferable because of His saying: ﴿But most of them turn away﴾, since turning away is not a attribute of believers. It was also said: "who know the language of the Arabs," so that they understand the Qur'an, since it is in their language. His saying ﴿for a people﴾ is connected either to "revelation" (tanzil) or to "were made clear" (fussilat), and the better view is that it is an attribute of "a Book." ﴿So they do not hear﴾ means they do not accept and do not obey; and this is expressed by not hearing, as an intensification (mubalaghah).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 5:

﴿In coverings﴾: plural of kinan (covering), which means a wrapping or cover. ﴿And between us and you there is a barrier﴾: an expression for their distance from Islam. ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: it has been said that its meaning is: act upon your religion, and we act upon our religion, so this is a disengagement (mutarakah). It has also been said: act in nullifying our affair, indeed we are acting in nullifying your affair, so this is a threat (tahdid).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 7:

﴿Those who do not give zakah, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾ It is the zakah of wealth. He singled it out for mention because it is difficult for people, and because it is one of the pillars of Islam. It was also said: by zakah is meant tawhid (monotheism), but this is far-fetched. What led to this view is that the verses are Meccan, and zakah was not made obligatory except in Medina. The answer is that what is meant is spending in obedience to Allah in general, and it had been commanded in Mecca.

﴿A reward never cut off﴾. That is, not cut off, from your saying "manantu al-habl" (I cut the rope) when you cut it. It is also said: not diminished. It is also said: not limited. And it is said: [Allah] does not confer it upon them as a favour (lā yamunnu ʿalayhim bihi), because conferring favours (al-mann) spoils the good deed.
﴿Andādan﴾ means equals and likenesses, such as idols and other things.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 41, verse 10:**

﴿Firm mountains﴾: meaning the mountains. ﴿And He blessed therein﴾: He increased its good. ﴿And measured therein its sustenance﴾: meaning the provisions of its inhabitants and their livelihood. It has also been said that it means the sustenance of the earth, such as minerals and other things by which the earth's existence is sustained. The first view is more apparent. ﴿In four days﴾: he means that the four days were completed by the first two days. He created the earth in two days and placed in it what was mentioned in two days, so that makes four days. He created the heavens in two days, so that makes six days, as mentioned in many places. Had these four days been in addition to the two days mentioned before them, the total would have been eight days, contrary to what is mentioned in many places. ﴿Equally﴾: the word is in the accusative (*sawa'an*) as a verbal noun (*masdar*), its implied meaning being "they became equal, an equality," as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn 'Atiyya said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) for "those who ask." It has been said that its meaning is "for those who ask about its matter," and it has been said that its meaning is "for those who seek it," and by seeking here is meant the creation's need for it. The prepositional phrase (*harf al-jarr*) is attached to an omitted element according to the first view, its implied meaning being: "He explains that to those who ask about it." According to the second view it is attached to *qaddara* ("measured").

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 11–12:

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, i.e., He directed Himself to it. This sequence (thumma) implies that the earth was created before the heaven. If it is asked: how is this reconciled with His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30]? The answer is that the earth was created before the heaven and then spread out afterwards. ﴿And it was smoke﴾. It is reported that the Throne was upon the water, and smoke was brought forth from the water and rose above the water. He dried the water and it became earth. Then He created the heavens from the rising smoke. ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come both of you willingly or unwillingly﴾. This is an expression of the obligation of their obedience, as a king says to one under his authority: "Do this, whether you wish or not," meaning: you must do it. It is also said that the meaning is: come willingly, or else you will be brought unwillingly. The meaning of this "coming" is their being shaped in the manner that God willed. His saying to them ﴿We came﴾ is a metaphor, an expression of His bringing them into being, and likewise their saying "We came obediently" is an expression that they did not resist Him when He willed their creation. It is also said that this is literal, and God caused the earth and the heaven to speak with their saying ﴿We came obediently﴾. The reason He used the plural form of the sound-minded (ta'if-een, "obedient") is that He described them with attributes of rational beings. ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾, i.e., He made them, and the pronoun refers to the seven heavens; their accusative is as a specification (tamyiz) explaining the pronoun. He referred back to them with the feminine plural pronoun because they do not reason; it is like your saying: "The trunks broke." Their being joined in the plural form of the thinking, rational being, in His saying ﴿obedient﴾, is because He described them with obedience, which is the act of rational beings, so He treated them as such. It is like His saying in Surah Yusuf [4]: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾. He used the dual pronoun in His saying ﴿They both said: We came﴾ because He made the earth one group and the heaven another. ﴿And He revealed in every heaven its affair﴾, i.e., He revealed to its inhabitants of angels, and to it itself, whatever He willed of matters by which its sustenance and welfare are maintained. He attributed the affair to it because it is in it. ﴿And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾, meaning the sun, the moon, and the stars, which are an adornment for the lowest heaven, whether they are in it or in what is above it of the heavens. ﴿And as protection﴾. Its implied sense is: and We protected it with protection. It may also be a object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), in meaning, as if He said: And We created the lamps as adornment and protection.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 41, verses 13–14:**

﴿But if they turn away﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh. ﴿a thunderbolt﴾: meaning one single, severe event. It is a metaphor drawn from the thunderbolt of fire. It is also read as *ṣaʿqah* with a sukun on the ʿayn, which is the event from your saying *ṣaʿiqa al-rajul* (the man was struck down). ﴿when the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them﴾: "before them" means what came earlier, and "behind them" means what came later. The meaning of the verse is that the messengers came to them in an earlier time, and their warning continued until the time of ʿAd and Thamud, so that the proof was established against them through that, "from before them." Then other messengers came to them when their lifespans were complete, and that is "from behind them." This is what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that they came to them from every direction, so it is an expression for their striving in delivering the message to them. It was also said: they informed them of what had befallen those before them, and that is "before them," and they warned them of what would befall them in the future time and in the Hereafter, and that is "from behind them." ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾: *an* here is a particle of explanation and interpretation, or it is a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, with the implied sense "that you not worship except Allah." ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾: this contains no acknowledgment by the disbelievers of the prophethood. Its meaning is rather "with what you were sent, according to your claim and your assertion," and it contains mockery.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿a furious wind, violently cold﴾... let me translate carefully below.

Translation:

﴿A violent, roaring wind﴾. It is said: it derives from ṣarr (ṣarr), which means intense cold, so the meaning is "cold." It is also said: it derives from your saying ṣarṣara, meaning it made a sound, so the meaning is that it has a terrifying sound. ﴿In ill-omened days﴾: the meaning is from naḥs (naḥs, ill-omened), which is the opposite of saʿd (saʿd, good fortune). It is also said: [they were] intensely cold. It is also said: [they were] successive. The first view is more preferred. It is narrated that they occurred in the last of Shawwal, from Wednesday to Wednesday. It was read as nuḥsāt with the ḥāʾ sukun and with kasra. As for the kasra, it is the plural of naḥs, which is a descriptive adjective. As for the sukun, it is a lightening of the kasra, on the pattern of fuʿl, or a description by means of the verbal noun.
"And as for Thamud, We guided them" — meaning: We made clear to them, so it has the sense of clarification (bayan), not the sense of guidance into the right path (irshad).

﴿فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾ meaning they are driven forcefully (yudfa'una bi-'unf). ﴿وَجُلُودُهُم﴾ meaning the well-known skins; it was said that it is a metaphor for the private parts, but the first view is more apparent. ﴿وَمَا كُنتُمْ تَسْتَتِرُونَ﴾ and the verses that follow may be understood as spoken by the skins, or by God Most High or by the angels. Regarding its meaning there are two views. The first: you could not conceal yourselves from your hearing, your sight and your skins, because they are constantly with you, so you had no way of guarding against them, and thus they bore witness against you. The second: you did not take precautions against the testimony of your hearing, sight and skins, because you did not care about their testimony and did not suppose that they would bear witness against you; you concealed yourselves only because you thought that God does not know much of what you do. This second view is preferred because it coheres with what follows it. This is also supported by the sound hadith from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Three men gathered, two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, little understanding in their hearts and much fat in their bellies, and they spoke a saying. One of them said: Do you think God hears what we say? Another said: He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we speak quietly. The third said: If He hears any of it, He hears all of it. Then the verse was revealed.

﴿أَرْدَاكُمْ﴾ meaning destroyed you; from al-radā (ruin), in the sense of destruction. ﴿وَإِن يَسْتَعْتِبُواْ فَمَا هُم مِّنَ ٱلْمُعْتَبِينَ﴾ this is from al-'atab in the sense of contentment, i.e. if they seek to be pleased, there is none among them who will be granted that. ﴿وَقَيَّضْنَا لَهُمْ قُرَنَآءَ﴾ meaning We made easy for them companions of evil, from the devils and the misguided among mankind. ﴿فَزَيَّنُواْ لَهُم مَّا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ﴾ "what is before them" is what preceded of their deeds, and "what is behind them" is what they are resolved upon; or "what is before them" is the affair of this world and "what is behind them" is the affair of the Hereafter, and denial of it. ﴿وَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقَوْلُ﴾ meaning the decree of their punishment had already been passed against them. ﴿فِيۤ أُمَمٍ﴾ meaning among a whole group of nations; it was said that "fi" here means "ma'a" (with).

﴿أَرْدَاكُمْ﴾ meaning destroyed you; from al-radā (ruin), in the sense of destruction. ﴿وَإِن يَسْتَعْتِبُواْ فَمَا هُم مِّنَ ٱلْمُعْتَبِينَ﴾ this is from al-'atab in the sense of contentment, i.e. if they seek to be pleased, there is none among them who will be granted that. ﴿وَقَيَّضْنَا لَهُمْ قُرَنَآءَ﴾ meaning We made easy for them companions of evil, from the devils and the misguided among mankind. ﴿فَزَيَّنُواْ لَهُم مَّا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ﴾ "what is before them" is what preceded of their deeds, and "what is behind them" is what they are resolved upon; or "what is before them" is the affair of this world and "what is behind them" is the affair of the Hereafter, and denial of it. ﴿وَحَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقَوْلُ﴾ meaning the decree of their punishment had already been passed against them. ﴿فِيۤ أُمَمٍ﴾ meaning among a whole group of nations; it was said that "fi" here means "ma'a" (with).

﴿فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾ meaning they are driven forcefully (yudfa'una bi-'unf). ﴿وَجُلُودُهُم﴾ meaning the well-known skins; it was said that it is a metaphor for the private parts, but the first view is more apparent. ﴿وَمَا كُنتُمْ تَسْتَتِرُونَ﴾ and the verses that follow may be understood as spoken by the skins, or by God Most High or by the angels. Regarding its meaning there are two views. The first: you could not conceal yourselves from your hearing, your sight and your skins, because they are constantly with you, so you had no way of guarding against them, and thus they bore witness against you. Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on Surah 41, verse 26:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may overcome."﴾ It is related that the one who uttered this statement was Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, may Allah curse him. ﴿And make noise during it﴾ means: do not listen to it, and occupy yourselves during its recitation with raising voices, reciting poetry, and the like, so that no one hears it. It was also said that the meaning is: engage in slander against it and find fault with it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 29–31:

﴿Show us those who misled us﴾ They say this when they enter Hellfire, so their saying is in the future but is expressed in the past tense. The meaning of "those who misled us" is everyone who led us astray from among the jinn and mankind. It was also said: what is meant is the son of Adam who instituted killing and Iblis who commanded disbelief and disobedience. This is false, because the son of Adam was a believer who disobeyed; rather, these people only ask for those who misled them into disbelief. ﴿We will put them under our feet﴾ meaning, in the lowest level of the Fire. ﴿Then they stood firm﴾ Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they stood firm upon their saying, "Our Lord is Allah," so their faith was sound and their monotheism endured. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: the meaning is that they stood firm in obedience and in abandoning sins. ʿUmar's saying is more complete and more cautious, but Abu Bakr's saying is preferred because of what was narrated from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "Some people who disbelieved said it; whoever dies upon it is among those who stood firm." Some Sufis said: the meaning of "they stood firm" is that they turned away from everything other than Allah, and this is the state of perfection, although the wording does not necessarily imply it. ﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ meaning at the time of death. ﴿And for you therein﴾ the pronoun refers to the Hereafter. ﴿Whatever you ask for﴾ meaning, whatever you desire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verses 33–35:

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾. Meaning: there is no one better in speech than him. This includes, in general, everyone who calls to the worship of Allah or to obedience to Him. It has also been said that the intended one is our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that it refers to the muezzins (the callers to prayer), but this is far-fetched, because the surah is Meccan, and the adhan was only legislated in Medina; nevertheless, the muezzins are included in the general meaning. ﴿And none receives it﴾: the pronoun refers to the beautiful character contained in His saying: ﴿Repel with that which is better﴾. ﴿Except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune﴾: meaning, one of great fortune in intellect and virtue. It has also been said: great fortune in Paradise.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 36–38:

﴿And if an incitement from Satan should cause you to waver﴾: "In" (إن) is a conditional particle, to which the superfluous "ma" (ما) has been attached. The "nazgh" of Satan (نزغ الشيطان) means his whisperings (وساوسه) and his commanding of evil (أمره بالسوء).

﴿He who created them﴾: The pronoun returns to the night, the day, the sun and the moon, because a plural of non-rational things is treated like a feminine plural, or like a single feminine noun. It was also said that it returns only to the sun and the moon, and that they were referred to in the plural because the dual is a plural. This is far-fetched.

﴿Then those who are with your Lord﴾: the angels, ﴿do not tire﴾, that is, they do not grow weary.

﴿The earth lying barren﴾ means a scarcity of vegetation. ﴿Then it stirs and swells﴾ is mentioned in al-Hajj [5]. ﴿Indeed, He who revived it is the Reviver of the dead﴾ is an illustration and an argument for the soundness of resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses﴾ meaning: they find fault with them. This deviation is by denial, and it was said: by idle talk about them, as was mentioned earlier in the surah. ﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ The verse. It was said that what is meant by the one thrown into the Fire is Abu Jahl, and by the one who comes secure is Uthman ibn Affan. It was also said: Ammar ibn Yasir. The wording is more general than that. ﴿Do whatever you wish﴾ is a threat, not a permission.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾: "the Reminder" (al-dhikr) here means the Qur'an, by consensus. The predicate of "inna" (indeed) is omitted, and its estimated form is: ﴿they have gone astray﴾, or they have perished. It was also said that its predicate is: ﴿those are called from a distant place﴾, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And indeed it is a Book of might﴾: that is, noble before God. It was also said: protected from Satan. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾: that is, nothing before it refutes it, and nothing that refutes it will come after it. The general meaning is that falsehood cannot reach it from any direction. ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾: this has two interpretations. The first: what God says to you of revelation and laws is only like what He said to the messengers before you. The second: what the disbelievers say to you of denial and harm is only like what the earlier nations said to their messengers. According to this second view, the meaning is consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) by following the example of earlier messengers. According to the first view, the meaning is that he (peace and blessings be upon him) brought what the messengers brought, so his messengership should not be denied. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness﴾: this may be a new sentence, or it may be the thing said in the previous verse. That applies to the first view. As for the second view, it is a new sentence, separate from what precedes it.

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾: "a'jami" (non-Arabic, or unable to speak clearly) is one who does not speak eloquently or clearly, whether he is from the Arabs or the non-Arabs. Also, "'ajami" is one who is not Arab, whether eloquent or not. The verse was revealed because the Quraysh criticized the Qur'an. So the meaning is: if it had been non-Arabic, they would have criticized it and said: "Why were its verses not made clear?" This shows that they would criticize it in any case. ﴿Would they not say, "Why were its verses not explained in detail? Is it a non-Arabic [book] and [the messenger] an Arab?"﴾: this is part of their speech. The interrogative hamza (ءَ) expresses denial. The meaning is: if the Qur'an were non-Arabic, they would say: "A non-Arabic Qur'an, and a messenger who is Arab, or sent to an Arab." It was also said that they only criticized it because of the non-Arabic words in it, such as sijjin and istabraq. So they said: "Is it a non-Arabic and Arabic Qur'an?", meaning mixed from the speech of Arabs and non-Arabs. This applies to the reading "a'jamiyyun" with a fatha on the 'ayn (عَجَمِيٌّ, read as a'jamiyyun with the vowel on the ʿayn).

﴿In their ears is deafness﴾: this expresses their turning away from the Qur'an, as if they were deaf and do not hear. Likewise, ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾ expresses how little they understand it. ﴿They are called from a distant place﴾: there are two views. The first: it is an expression for how little they understand, so they are likened to one who is called from a distant place, who cannot hear the voice nor grasp what is said. The second: it is literal, on the Day of Resurrection, that is, they will be called from a distant place so that the people of the gathering may hear their rebuke. ﴿In their ears is deafness﴾: this expresses their turning away from the Qur'an, as if they were deaf and do not hear. Likewise, ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾ expresses how little they understand it. ﴿They are called from a distant place﴾: there are two views. The first: it is an expression for how little they understand, so they are likened to one who is called from a distant place, who cannot hear the voice nor grasp what is said. The second: it is literal, on the Day of Resurrection, that is, they will be called from a distant place so that the people of the gathering may hear their rebuke. The first is more fitting with the metaphors that precede it.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾: "the Reminder" (al-dhikr) here means the Qur'an, by consensus. The predicate of "inna" (indeed) is omitted, and its estimated form is: ﴿they have gone astray﴾, or they have perished. It was also said that its predicate is: ﴿those are called from a distant place﴾, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And indeed it is a Book of might﴾: that is, noble before God. It was also said: protected from Satan. ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it﴾: that is, nothing before it refutes it, and nothing that refutes it will come after it. The general meaning is that falsehood cannot reach it from any direction. ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾: this has two interpretations. The first: what God says to you of revelation and laws is only like what He said to the messengers before you. The second: what the disbelievers say to you of denial and harm is only like what the earlier nations said to their messengers. According to this second view, the meaning is consoling the Prophet (ﷺ) by following the example of earlier messengers. According to the first view, the meaning is that he (peace and blessings be upon him) brought what the messengers brought, so his messengership should not be denied. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness﴾: this may be a new sentence, or it may be the thing said in the previous verse. That applies to the first view. As for the second view, it is a new sentence, separate from what precedes it.

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾: "a'jami" (non-Arabic, or unable to speak clearly) is one who does not speak eloquently or clearly, whether he is from the Arabs or the non-Arabs. Also, "'ajami" is one who is not Arab, whether eloquent or not. The verse was revealed because the Quraysh criticized the Qur'an. So the meaning is: if it had been non-Arabic, they would have criticized it and said: "Why were its verses not made clear?" This shows that they would criticize it in any case. ﴿Would they not say, "Why were its verses not explained in detail? Is it a non-Arabic [book] and [the messenger] an Arab?"﴾: this is part of their speech. The interrogative hamza (ءَ) expresses denial. The meaning is: if the Qur'an were non-Arabic, they would say: "A non-Arabic Qur'an, and a messenger who is Arab, or sent to an Arab." It was also said that they only criticized it because of the non-Arabic words in it, such as sijjin and istabraq. So they said: "Is it a non-Arabic and Arabic Qur'an?", meaning mixed from the speech of Arabs and non-Arabs. This applies to the reading "a'jamiyyun" with a fatha on the 'ayn (عَجَمِيٌّ, read as a'jamiyyun with the vowel on the ʿayn).

﴿In their ears is deafness﴾: this expresses their turning away from the Qur'an, as if they were deaf and do not hear. Likewise, ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾ expresses how little they understand it. ﴿They are called from a distant place﴾: there are two views. The first: it is an expression for how little they understand, so they are likened to one who is called from a distant place, who cannot hear the voice nor grasp what is said. The second: it is literal, on the Day of Resurrection, that is, they will be called from a distant place so that the people of the gathering may hear their rebuke. The first is more fitting with the metaphors that precede it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 45:

﴿A word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾ means: the decree (al-qadr).

﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾, meaning the knowledge of the time of its occurrence. So if anyone is asked about that, he says: Allah is the One who knows it. ﴿From within their sheaths﴾: the plural of *kumm* (كم, a sheath, the covering of the fruit before it appears), with a kasra on the kaf.

﴿And the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾ The governing element of "the day" is omitted, and what is meant is the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun refers to the polytheists. His saying, ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, is a rebuke to them. He attributed the partners to Himself according to the assumption of the polytheists, as if He said: the partners whom you made for Me. ﴿They will say, "We have informed You that none of us bears witness."﴾ The meaning is that they say: "We have informed You that none of us witnesses today that You have a partner," because they disowned their partners on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 48:

﴿And that which they used to invoke before has strayed from them,﴾ meaning: their partners have strayed from them, in the sense that they do not see them at that time, so "ma" in this reading is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). Or it means: their former speech, the polytheism they used to utter, has strayed from them, so "ma" in this reading is a verbal noun (masdariyyah). ﴿And they will think that there is for them no place of escape.﴾ The word "zann" (thought, supposition) here carries the meaning of "yaqin" (certainty), and "mahis" means refuge or place of escape: that is, they knew that there was no escape for them from the punishment. It has also been said that one should stop at "zannu" (wa-zannu), and that "ma lahum" begins a new sentence (isti'naf), but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 49:

﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾. That is, he does not grow weary of asking for wealth, well-being, and the like. The verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, though it was also said to concern others among the disbelievers. The wording, however, is more general than that.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verse 50:

﴿Surely he will say, "This is mine (by right)"﴾ That is, "This is my due right, and it is not a favour from Allah. Only a disbeliever says this." This is shown by His words: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come to be﴾, and His words: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely with Him there will be the best (reward) for me﴾. Its meaning is: "If I am raised again, there will be Paradise for me." This is conjecture and arrogance. It is related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

﴿And He turns away with His side﴾ — mentioned in al-Isra' [83] — meaning, he is abundant (in ingratitude). Allah mentions these traits in order to censure them.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ (Surah Fussilat 41:52)

The meaning of the verse: Tell me, if the Qur'an is from Allah and you then disbelieve in it, are you not in extreme opposition (shiqaq ba'id)? He placed the phrase "who is further astray" (man aḍall) in place of addressing them directly.

Note on the translation of "فوضع قوله (من أحل)": this phrase reads literally as "he placed his saying (man aḍall)", where "man aḍall" is the Qur'anic wording "من أضل" in verse 52, not "من أحل". The text as written is the transmitted reading of the commentary and I have rendered it as it stands.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 41, verses 53–54:

﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves﴾. The pronoun refers to the Quraysh. There are three opinions on this. The first is that the signs on the horizons are the conquest of the regions for the Muslims, and the signs within themselves are the conquest of Makkah. Thus this combines a promise to the Muslims of victory, a threat to the disbelievers, and an argument against them through the manifestation of the truth and the abasement of falsehood. The second is that the signs on the horizons are what befell the earlier nations of destruction, and the signs within themselves are the Day of Badr. The third is that the signs on the horizons are the creation of the heavens and what is in them of lessons and signs, and the signs within themselves are the creation of the children of Adam. This opinion is weak, because He said ﴿We will show them﴾ with the sin of the future tense, and the heavens and the creation of the children of Adam were already visible. The first opinion is the preferred one. ﴿That it is the truth﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an or to Islam. ﴿Encompassing﴾, i.e., encompassing by His knowledge, His power and His authority.
